name: Moklen
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat & Songphan Choemprayong. 2024. A proposal for a Thai-based Moklen orthography. Language Documentation & Conservation 18: 194-215. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. hdl:10125/74803 (open access, CC BY-NC).
catalog_locator: Sect. 3 'Phoneme inventory of Moklen', pp. 198-199 (prosodic-word/stress statement and Table 2), p. 200 (18 vowels in stressed vs 5 + extra-short /ə/ in unstressed syllables), p. 201 (word-tone statement).
catalog_quote: The prosodic word in Moklen must be exactly one iambic foot. That is, it may consist of either one stressed heavy monosyllable or an unstressed light syllable followed by a stressed heavy one. Furthermore, the stressed syllable may be an open syllable with a long vowel or a closed syllable with either a short or long vowel. In contrast, the unstressed syllable must always be open. Interestingly, simplex words in Moklen are overwhelmingly disyllables, with very strong preference for CV.ˈCVC and CV.ˈCVVC. [pp. 198-199] ... Unusual for Austronesian languages, Moklen has a total of eighteen vowels in stressed syllables, comprising nine pairs of short and long ones. However, the vowel length contrast is crucially completely neutralized in the initial syllable of disyllabic words. In other words, only /a/, /i/, /u/, /ɔ/, and /ɛ/ can occur in unstressed syllables. [p. 200] ... Moklen can thus be considered a language with word tones, as each prosodic word can only bear one tone on the stressed syllables. The initial syllables of disyllables are always phonologically toneless. Quantitatively speaking, the tonal contrast is marginal as few minimal pairs exist. [p. 201]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text, pp.5-6 = journal pp.198-199, and p.8 = p.201). The quoted passage is there word for word: p.198-199 'The prosodic word in Moklen must be exactly one iambic foot. That is, it may consist of either one stressed heavy monosyllable or an unstressed light syllable followed by a stressed heavy one. Interestingly, simplex words in Moklen are overwhelmingly disyllables, with very strong preference for CV.ˈCVC and CV.ˈCVVC.' and p.201 'Moklen can thus be considered a language with word to…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable: every prosodic word is a single iambic foot, either a stressed heavy monosyllable or an unstressed open light syllable plus a stressed heavy final syllable; the (marginal, two-way) lexical tone contrast and the full 18-vowel inventory are licensed only on that stressed final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in Pittayaporn & Choemprayong (initial syllable simply 'unstressed', toneless, reduced vowel set /a i u ɔ ɛ ə/). Loss 2023:3 transcribes citation forms with a secondary-stress mark on the minor syllable (ˌtəˈʔáw 'sea', ˌkaˈbáːŋ 'boat') but elsewhere (p.28) calls the minor syllable unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions stated; words are maximally disyllabic (one foot). Variation concerns the unstressed initial syllable (four variant shapes, /ba-/~/ma-/, /ʔɔ-/~[ʔa-]) and its optional loss in connected speech/compounds ('monosyllabic alternants', Loss 2023), never stress placement. Thai loans are numerous (marked with Thai tone numbers in Loss 2023) but no different stress behaviour is described.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = one iambic foot; statements based on citation forms from Bangsak (Phang Nga) fieldwork 2017-2021 ('In citation forms, Tone 1 is realized..'). Corroborated independently by Loss 2023:28 ('the second major syllable receives primary stress while the initial minor syllable is unstressed') and by the instrumental study Pornpottanamas et al. 2023:59 ('an iambic language that assigns stress to the last syllable of the foot.. the ultimate syllable, which is always stressed').
new_statements.identity_note: All modern first-hand sources downloaded (Pittayaporn & Choemprayong 2024, Loss 2023, Pornpottanamas et al. 2023, Maspong et al. 2024) describe the Moklen [mkm, mokl1243] variety of Bangsak / Thap Tawan area, Takua Pa district, Phang Nga province (Pittayaporn & Choemprayong say its sound system 'generally agrees with descriptions by Swastham (1982) and Larish (1997; 1999; 2005)'). Not to be confused with sister language Moken (moke1242), already in the catalog with the same iambic/final-stress pattern. Note the language is described as having a marginal two-way lexical (word-)tone contrast realized on the stressed final syllable, so the reading is 'tone language with a stress statement' with stress itself fixed: final syllable (iambic).

tone_statements.citation: Court, Christopher. 1971. A fleeting encounter with the Moken (the sea gypsies) in southern Thailand: some linguistic and general notes. Journal of the Siam Society 59(1): 83-95.
tone_statements.quote: Syllable pitch seems to depend largely on the position of a word in an utterance. Thus most words were said with a falling pitch when given as single-word answers to a question. This is a common feature in non-tonal languages such as, for example, English. One or two words, however, seemed to be quite fixed in their pitch patterns under all circumstances, e.g., [bah] the negative particle, and [lualJ] '(?)' in [ni?Ctn lilaiJ] 'young coconut' and the personal names [khiaw (<Thai?), nan, til:, biiJ, na: lJ].
tone_statements.locator: p. 87 (paragraph after the charts of contoids, vocoids and pitch levels; JSS 59(1)); see also p. 86 ('appear to have a fixed tone') and p. 93, 'Typologically interesting features'
tone_statements.summary: 1970 field notes: pitch judged mostly intonational (falling in citation), i.e. apparently non-tonal, but a handful of words with lexically fixed pitch - incipient/marginal tone noticed, no inventory (later work: 2 lexical tones, low functional load).

sources.citation: Maspong, Sireemas, Francesco Burroni, et al. 2024. Leveraging deep learning to shed light on tones of an endangered language: a case study of Moklen. Proc. Field Matters 2024 (ACL), doi:10.18653/v1/2024.fieldmatters-1.5
sources.note: p.2 background: 'Two features.. shared by Moklen and other MSEA languages, are systematic word-final stress and tonal contrast. Moklen follows a consistent iambic stress pattern, with stress assigned to the last syllable of the foot (Larish, 1999; Swastham, 1982). Moklen tones are consistently realized only on the ultimate syllable, which also bears stress.'
